India concluded a major long-term uranium-supply agreement in 2026 as part of its attempt to
expand nuclear-power generation and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. The agreement was
signed during the Canadian prime minister’s visit to India and marked a significant
improvement in relations between the two countries after a period of diplomatic tension.

Under the agreement, a leading Canadian uranium producer will supply uranium concentrate
to India for use in its civilian nuclear-reactor fleet. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2027
and continue for almost a decade. The arrangement is among India’s largest long-term
nuclear-fuel procurement contracts.

The agreement supports India’s objective of increasing its nuclear-power capacity to 100 GW
by 2047. India presently depends substantially on coal for electricity generation, while its
domestic uranium resources are limited in quantity and quality. Imported uranium can
support the operation of safeguarded civilian reactors while India continues developing its
indigenous three-stage nuclear programme.

India’s ability to participate in international nuclear commerce is closely connected with the
India–United States Civil Nuclear Agreement negotiated during the 2000s. That agreement
led India to separate its civilian and military nuclear facilities and place designated civilian
facilities under international safeguards.

India subsequently obtained a country-specific waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group. The
waiver permitted participating countries to engage in civilian nuclear trade with India even
though India had not joined the principal international treaty governing nuclear non-
proliferation.

The 2026 uranium agreement should therefore be understood as an India–Canada supply
arrangement operating within the international nuclear-trade framework made possible by the
earlier India–US civil nuclear initiative.

Ladakh underwent a significant administrative reorganisation in 2026 when five new districts
were formally notified. The decision increased the number of districts in the Union Territory
from two to seven and was intended to improve governance in geographically remote areas
where residents often travelled considerable distances to access public services.

The creation of the districts had originally been approved by the Union Ministry of Home
Affairs in August 2024. Their territorial boundaries, headquarters and revenue villages were
subsequently finalised, enabling the Ladakh administration to issue the formal notification in
April 2026.

Three of the new districts were carved out of the former territory of Leh district, while two
were created from Kargil district. Each district was provided with a designated headquarters
for its administrative offices. The reorganisation was accompanied by proposals for new
tehsils, sub-tehsils, patwar circles and district-level government posts.

The creation of administrative districts did not automatically create elected representative
bodies in each district. Ladakh initially continued to have only the two Autonomous Hill
Development Councils that existed before the reorganisation. The administration
subsequently announced that the hill-council system would be extended to all seven districts.

The councils are intended to promote democratic decentralisation by giving elected
representatives a role in district-level planning, development and administration. Their
responsibilities include matters relating to land, local infrastructure, agriculture, public health,

The proposal is particularly significant because Ladakh is a Union Territory without a
legislative assembly. Hill councils consequently provide one of the principal mechanisms for
elected local representation. However, they are statutory bodies created under parliamentary
legislation and are different from the autonomous district councils established under the Sixth
Schedule of the Constitution.

Before the additional councils become fully operational, the administration must complete
measures including any necessary statutory amendments, delimitation of territorial
constituencies, notification of council areas and the conduct of elections.

Protests against the Ken–Betwa River-Linking Project intensified in Madhya Pradesh in
2026, with project-affected families demanding fair compensation, proper rehabilitation,
recognition of forest rights and greater transparency in land acquisition.

The protesters, many of whom belong to the Gond and Kol tribal communities, adopted
several symbolic methods of resistance. These included lying on mock funeral pyres,
standing in water, observing hunger strikes, placing symbolic nooses around their necks and
suspending cooking in affected villages. Women played a prominent role in the
demonstrations.

The July phase of the agitation was organised on the bank of a river near a village in
_________ district. Police subsequently cleared the demonstration site, citing rising water
levels and safety concerns. The protest leader, who had been on an indefinite fast, was moved
to a hospital. Protesters alleged that the police had detained participants, while the authorities
denied making formal arrests.

The project is intended to transfer water from the Ken basin to the Betwa basin through a
dam, tunnel and canal system. The government argues that the project will provide irrigation
and drinking water to the drought-prone Bundelkhand region while also generating
hydroelectric and solar power.

Opponents question the classification of the Ken as a “surplus” river and argue that the
project will submerge forests, displace thousands of families and affect wildlife habitats.
Particular concern has been expressed regarding the submergence and fragmentation of an
important tiger reserve that underwent a successful tiger-reintroduction programme after its
tiger population had disappeared.

The project consists of multiple components implemented in two phases. Its principal
component is a large dam across the Ken River. Other components include barrages and
irrigation projects in the upper Betwa basin.

The controversy illustrates the wider conflict between large infrastructure projects and the
rights of communities dependent on land and forests. It also raises questions regarding
whether environmental compensation and wildlife-management plans can adequately replace
mature natural ecosystems.

People fortunate to have dogs will insist, not even half-jokingly, that their “baby” can
understand every word they utter. Rover can identify his favourite toy, and Moti will run across
rooms when he hears the word “chicken” (or whatever the puppy’s favourite food happens to
be). In essence, many dog parents — like the parents of some human children — insist that
their baby is secretly brilliant. But in at least one sense, pet dogs had it better than human kids.
No dog mom or dad has ever compared their canine companion unfavourably to the
neighbour’s pooch or complained about them being underachievers. The pride in the so-called
intelligence of their pets can be put down to blind affection. That could change.

A study published in Science last week has made global headlines. Researchers found that
Gifted Word Learner dogs can “acquire novel words by overhearing third-party interactions”
in much the same way that human toddlers do. Not only can these genius dogs label hundreds
of items, they can also pick up vocabulary by eavesdropping on human conversations.
Labelling, linguists and behaviourists will rush to clarify, it isn’t the same as language — in all
its grammatical, lexical and metaphorical complexity. But the study does indicate that non-
human animals can learn in the same ways we do, and perhaps carry within them multitudes
we do not yet comprehend.

But in all this talk of meaning and science, language and being, little thought is being given to
poor Rover and Moti. The study, after all, focuses on the rare, “gifted” dogs. Most are still just
a best friend, loving their people unconditionally. Let’s hope that those parents who want their
kids to be toppers and brilliant, who push them to be cutthroat in a dog-eat-dog world, spoil
the dog — even if they couldn’t spare the child

A cruel battle was being fought. The ground was covered with dead and dying men. The air
was hot and stifling. The sun shone down without pity on the wounded soldiers lying in the
blood and dust.


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                      13

12 Minutes to CLAT                                                 CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 31

One of these soldiers was a no-ble-man, whom everybody loved for his gen-tle-ness and
kindness. Yet now he was no better off than the poorest man in the field. He had been wounded,
and would die, and he was suffering much with pain and thirst.

When the battle was over, his friends hurried to his aid. A soldier came running with a cup in
his hand.

"Here, Sir Philip," he said, "I have brought you some clear, cool water from the brook. I will
raise your head so that you can drink."

The cup was placed to Sir Philip's lips. How thank-ful-ly he looked at the man who had brought
it! Then his eyes met those of a dying soldier who was lying on the ground close by. The wistful
look in the poor man's face spoke plainer than words.

"Give the water to that man," said Sir Philip quickly, and then, pushing the cup toward him, he
said, "Here, my comrade, take this. Thy need is greater than mine."

What a brave, noble man he was! The name of Sir Philip Sidney will never be forgotten; for it
was the name of a Christian gentleman who always had the good of others in his mind. Was it
any wonder that everybody wept when it was heard that he was dead? It is said, that, on the
day when he was carried to the grave, every eye in the land was filled with tears. Rich and
poor, high and low, all felt that they had lost a friend; all mourned the death of the kindest,
gentlest man that they had ever known.

Last year, India bought 1.8L electric cars, 77% over 2024. But in terms of overall car sales this
amounted to just 3.8%. Clearly, 10 years of govt incentives and subsidies haven’t convinced
buyers of the advantages of going electric. Two reasons are obvious: range anxiety + inadequate
charging infra, and high prices + limited choice at the lower end. Low sales, by global
standards, aren’t allowing the Indian EV ecosystem to mature. This explains Indian carmakers’
dread of cheap Chinese EVs slipping in via EU after an FTA. But there’s a counterview. Let
EVs of every ilk come in freely and cheaply. Growing EV popularity will automatically spur
growth of charging and servicing infra, which means more jobs. After all, countries that don’t
make any cars at all, like Australia, also have well-developed fuelling and charging networks.



                                  12minutestoclat.com                                         15

12 Minutes to CLAT                                                CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 31

This infra boost will serve domestic carmakers too if they raise their technology game with
R&D, like China did.

But to go on pushing domestic EV sales with subsidies and mandates is pointless. For example,
what will Telangana’s plan to make schools induct 25-50% EVs in their vehicle fleets lead to?
Greater burden on parents. Electric buses cost far more than diesel or gas buses, and because
school buses run for only a couple of hours daily, gains on the air-quality front will be minimal.
Far better to focus on city bus fleets that run from morning to night.

EV subsidies, like Delhi’s ₹1L benefit for 27,000 electric cars priced up to ₹25L, are
questionable on several counts. Who gains from them? The rich. Who’s hurt by the revenue
loss? The poor. Those crores are better used to ensure potable water and sewage don’t mix,
right? A Harvard Law School study found subsidies only encourage the rich to buy EVs as their
non-primary vehicles, worsening urban congestion and pollution. Other studies have shown
that when the government subsidises electric cars, manufacturers have no incentive to lower
prices. Without subsidies, they would have to raise prices on their non-EV cars to offset the
discounts they offer on EVs Let the market work, and save public funds for the public.

The new US ambassador to India Sergio Gor said on Monday that an amicable Indo-US trade
deal is very much in the realm of the possible and even the larger Indo-US partnership continues
to be robust. These pages have always underlined the importance of patiently pursuing
economic and diplomatic dialogue with the US rather than getting distracted by the shrill
rhetoric coming from Washington. Such a policy approach, however, will also have to keep in



                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       17

mind the fact that the days of the US being an open export market to even its closest allies are
almost over and the quid pro quo element in such a relationship will be bigger than the past.

In this context, it is extremely important that India cultivate its economic relations with Europe.
It is a large trading block with consumers who have the highest purchasing power anywhere
outside the US, is also feeling the pinch of the about turn in US’s policies, and is also invested
in looking at India as a stakeholder in maintaining a rules-based democratic framework in the
world unlike an increasingly imperialist US or authoritarian China. The more than 14% jump
in Indian exports to Europe in November — to almost $8 billion — is a welcome development
on this front. To be sure, not much should be read into a month’s trade numbers, and it is worth
noting that Indian exports to Europe fell by more than a billion dollars year on year in October.

However, what makes even a short-term reading of Indo-European trade numbers important is
that trade negotiations are still continuing at multiple levels. A successful and mutually
beneficial conclusion of a trade agreement can very well set a new benchmark for democracies
doing trade well.

as America’s underlying strategic interest. This twin focus on Russian sanctions and
Venezuelan oil assets suggests that both measures are less about geopolitical ‘penalisation’ and
more about protecting the petrodollar’s dominance at a time when its hegemony is eroding. For

The freedom to carry on trade, business, occupation or profession under clause (1)(g) of Article
19 protects engagement in games in which skill predominates over chance, since such games
have long been treated as a legitimate commercial activity rather than gambling. This
protection, however, does not extend to betting or wagering, an activity classified as res extra
commercium, meaning it stands wholly outside the constitutional guarantee of trade and cannot
be claimed as a matter of right, however substantial the underlying skill.

Once a stake, being money or property staked upon an uncertain outcome, is introduced into
the play of any game, the activity acquires the character of betting notwithstanding that the
game itself, considered without the wager, would ordinarily be recognised as one of skill; the
relevant enquiry thereupon ceases to be whether skill predominates over chance and becomes
instead whether a stake was risked on the result.

A State Legislature is accordingly competent under Entry 34 of List II of the Seventh Schedule
to prohibit, and not merely regulate, betting connected with any game, including a game that
would otherwise qualify for constitutional protection, since the constitutional immunity
historically extended to skill-based play is a legislative choice rather than a compulsion binding

Chapter V of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 imposes obligations styled 'certain relations
resembling those created by contract' upon persons who have received a benefit at another's
expense, even where no agreement, offer or acceptance ever passed between them; liability
rests not upon consent but upon the equitable principle that no person ought to be enriched
unjustly at the cost of another.

Where necessaries suited to the condition in life of a person incapable of contracting, or of any
dependant whom such person is legally bound to support, are supplied to that incapable person,
the supplier is entitled to be reimbursed out of the property of the incapable person; no personal
liability attaches to the incapable person, and recourse lies solely against his estate, if any.

Where a person, though lawfully doing something for another or delivering something to
another, does not intend to act gratuitously, and the other person accepts and enjoys the benefit
of the act or the thing so delivered, the latter is bound to compensate the former or to restore
the thing so delivered; this obligation, however, does not arise merely because a benefit has in
fact accrued, for it presupposes both that the actor did not intend gratuity and that the recipient
had a genuine opportunity to decline the benefit before it was thrust upon him, since a person
who enjoys a benefit conferred without any real choice in the matter incurs no obligation to
compensate.

Separately, a person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake, whether
of law or of fact, or under coercion, is bound to repay or return it, this obligation being
unaffected by whether the payer's mistaken belief concerned a question of fact or a question of

An act does not amount to an offence if the person doing it was, at the time of doing it,
incapable, by reason of unsoundness of mind, either of knowing the nature of the act, or of
knowing that the act was wrong or contrary to law; either species of incapacity suffices
independently, and an accused is not required to establish both.

The law begins with a presumption that every person is of sound mind and accountable for his
acts, so that the burden of displacing this presumption rests upon the accused, who need only
establish unsoundness of the requisite degree on a preponderance of probabilities, a materially
lighter standard than the prosecution's own burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

12 Minutes to CLAT                                               CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 31

The unsoundness relied upon must be shown to have existed precisely at the moment the act
was committed; evidence of insanity before or after that moment, including a subsequent lucid

incapacity at that moment.

Section 3 of the Competition Act, 2002 renders void any agreement between enterprises that
causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India.
Agreements among enterprises engaged at the same stage of production or trade, such as
arrangements to fix prices, limit or control output, allocate markets or customers, or rig bids,
are presumed to cause such an adverse effect, and this presumption may be displaced only
where the enterprises establish that the arrangement constitutes a joint venture that increases
efficiency in production, supply, distribution or control of goods or services.

Agreements between enterprises operating at different stages of the same production or
distribution chain, including exclusive supply obligations, exclusive distribution arrangements,
refusal to deal and resale price maintenance, attract no such presumption; their legality is
instead tested under a rule of reason, requiring an affirmative demonstration of appreciable
adverse effect having regard to factors including barriers to new entry, foreclosure of existing
competitors and any countervailing benefit accruing to consumers.

Separately, Section 4 prohibits not dominance as such, which is lawful and indeed the natural
consequence of legitimate commercial success, but only the abuse of a dominant position once
such dominance is established. Establishing abuse accordingly proceeds in two distinct stages:
first, the relevant market, defined along both product and geographic dimensions, must be
delineated and the enterprise's dominance within that market ascertained with reference to
market share, countervailing buying power and entry barriers, none of which is by itself a
conclusive numerical threshold; and only thereafter does the enquiry turn to whether the
dominant enterprise's conduct amounts to an abuse of that established dominance.

Conduct identical in form, such as an exclusive supply obligation, may accordingly fall to be
examined either under the rule of reason applicable to vertical agreements or under the abuse-
of-dominance framework, depending entirely on whether the enterprise imposing it is shown
to hold a dominant position in the relevant market.
